pl-l4d49c1-d1e115.summary: States, after Augustine, that after the resurrection and the completed judgment the two cities will have their ends, one Christ's, the other the devil's, of good and bad, angels and men; the good will lack the will to sin, the bad the power to sin or die; the one living happily in eternal life, the other unhappily in eternal death without the power to die, both without end; but some of the blessed more excellently, and some of the wretched more tolerably.
claims: The two cities are eternally separated.
Both bliss and misery have degrees.

pl-l4d49c1-d1e121.summary: Draws out that as the good will be glorified differently, so the wicked will be punished differently: as there are many mansions, differences of reward, in the Father's house, so in hell differences of punishment; yet all suffer eternal punishment, as all the elect receive the same denarius given to all the vineyard workers, eternal life, God himself, enjoyed by all but unequally. As bodies will be differently glorified, so souls; star differs from star; some will contemplate God's form more nearly and clearly, and this difference is called the diversity of mansions; one house, one denarius, many mansions. All will enjoy God by sight, not in a mirror; to have life is to see life, to know God by sight: 'this is eternal life, that they know you'.
claims: Degrees of punishment answer degrees of glory.
All the elect enjoy God, the one denarius, unequally.
The many mansions are degrees of vision.
Eternal life is knowing God by sight.

pl-l4d49c1-d1e149.summary: Asks whether all will beatitude and know what true beatitude is.

pl-l4d49c1-d1e152.summary: Quotes Augustine: it is wonderful that, though the will to attain and keep beatitude is one in all, there is such diversity of wills about it, not that anyone does not want it, but not all know it; if all knew, some would not place it in virtue of mind, others in bodily pleasure; how can all love what not all know? Perhaps all know what it is but not where it is.
claims: All will happiness but disagree about what it is.

pl-l4d49c1-d1e164.summary: Continues Augustine: perhaps it is false that all want to live happily; if happy life is living by virtue, one who does not want that does not want happiness; but Cicero did not doubt that all want to be happy; yet to say that one who does not want to live by virtue wants to live happily seems absurd, a contradiction; how then do all want to live happily if not all want to live as alone one lives happily?

pl-l4d49c1-d1e170.summary: Continues Augustine: is happiness living by one's delight? No, to will what is unfitting is most miserable, worse than not obtaining what one wills; the evil will alone makes one wretched, more so when fulfilled. Since all want happiness and cannot love what they do not know, all know the happy life; the happy have what they want, but not all who have what they want are happy; the happy have all they want and want nothing badly; and though one may be good among evils, he is not happy until all evils end.
claims: Happiness is having all one wills and willing nothing badly.
Fulfilling an evil will is worse than failing.
No one is happy until all evils end.

pl-l4d49c1-d1e182.summary: Concludes Augustine: when the faithful and good come from this life to the blessed one, it will be true, as it cannot be now, that man lives as he wills; he will not will to live badly, nor lack what he wills, nor will what is lacking; all loved will be present, nothing desired absent; all good, God the highest good, and, most blessed, certain forever. All want to be happy, but not all have the faith by which happiness is reached.
claims: In heaven one lives as one wills, willing only the good.
Faith is the way to happiness.

pl-l4d49c1.summary: After the judgment the two cities, of Christ and of the devil, will have their ends: the good without will, the wicked without power to sin or die, the one living happily in eternal life, the other in eternal death, both without end, but with degrees: the good differently glorified, the wicked differently punished, as there are many mansions in the Father's house and in hell. All the elect receive the same denarius, eternal life, God himself, enjoyed unequally, as star differs from star; the many mansions are degrees of vision of God, life being to know God by sight. Asked whether all want beatitude and know what it is, Augustine argues all will to be happy and so in some sense know it; the happy man has all he wants and wants nothing badly, which is possible only when all evils end; in the blessed life no one will will evil or lack anything he wills, and the highest good, God, will be secure forever.
claims: After the judgment the two cities reach their ends, both eternal.
All the elect enjoy God, the common denarius, but unequally.
Eternal life is knowing God by sight.
All will happiness; only the blessed have all they will and will nothing badly.
